details:
**Baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist in the Jordan River**
John the Baptist, son of Elizabeth and a relative of Jesus, baptized Jesus in the Jordan River. As Jesus came up from the water, the Holy Spirit descended on him "like a dove," and a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." The event is the First Luminous Mystery of the Rosary and is celebrated at Theophany (Epiphany) in Eastern churches; John said that Jesus would baptize "with the Holy Spirit."

**Great Commission and the Trinitarian formula**
In Matthew 28:19, the risen Jesus commands his disciples to "make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Most churches therefore require this Trinitarian formula for a valid baptism, though some "Oneness" churches baptize in the name of Jesus only.

**Baptism for the dead (Mormons)**
Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints perform proxy baptisms in temples on behalf of the deceased, citing 1 Corinthians 15:29 ("Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead?"). The practice caused controversy when it was performed for Holocaust victims such as Anne Frank, and early church writers attributed a similar vicarious baptism to the Marcionites.

**Anabaptists and believer's baptism**
Radical Reformation groups such as the Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites rejected infant baptism as meaningless, because infants cannot understand or profess faith. They "re-baptized" adults, earning the name Anabaptists. Believer's baptism (credobaptism) for people who have reached the "age of accountability," often by full immersion, is also practiced by Baptist churches such as the Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in the U.S.

**Baptism of blood and baptism of desire**
Catholic doctrine holds that people who die before being baptized with water can still receive its grace. Baptism of blood, defended by Cyprian of Carthage, applies to unbaptized martyrs who die for the faith, and baptism of desire applies to those who sincerely wished for it; the Good Thief, Dismas, is often cited as an example. The Jesuit Leonard Feeney's denial of these forms, insisting that only water baptism saves, was condemned, and his view is called Feeneyism.

**Aspersion, affusion, and immersion**
The three methods of baptism: aspersion is sprinkling water on the person, affusion is pouring water over the head, and immersion is dipping the whole body. Eastern Orthodox churches baptize even infants by triple immersion, once for each person of the Trinity, and water is held in a baptismal font.

**Infant baptism (christening) and original sin**
Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, and many other churches baptize infants, a rite often called christening because the child is also named. Baptism is the first sacrament of initiation in Catholicism and is believed to wash away original sin; in an emergency, any person can validly baptize.

**Ulrich Zwingli's symbolic view**
The Swiss Reformer Huldrych Zwingli argued that baptism is a symbolic sign of belonging to the covenant community rather than a means of grace. He still defended infant baptism, and his followers broke with him over it to form the first Anabaptist movement. By contrast, John Calvin described baptism as being "engrafted into Christ."

**Mandaeans and yardna**
The Mandaeans, a Gnostic religion of Iraq and Iran that honors John the Baptist, perform baptism (masbuta) repeatedly as a purification ritual in flowing "living" water. They call such water yardna, a word derived from the Jordan River.

**Renouncing Satan, "his works and pomps"**
In the baptismal vows, the candidate or the godparents answer "I do renounce" when asked to reject Satan, "all his works," and "all his pomps." Catholics renew these baptismal promises, for example at the Easter Vigil.

**Elcesaites and rabies**
The Elcesaites (Elkasaites), an early Jewish-Christian sect, reportedly practiced repeated baptisms, including as a cure for people bitten by rabid dogs.

**Tevilah and the mikvah**
Christian baptism is often traced to tevilah, the Jewish rite of full immersion for purification in a ritual bath called a mikvah, which is also used in conversion to Judaism. Comparable initiation rites in other faiths include the Sikh Amrit Sanchar and the Zoroastrian Navjote, at which initiates receive the sudreh (sacred shirt) and kusti (sacred cord).

**Catechumens and the baptismal font**
Catechumens are people receiving religious instruction to prepare for baptism. Baptism takes place at a font, sometimes in a separate building called a baptistery; in medieval Italy, rural churches called pievi had their own fonts, so people did not have to travel to the cathedral.

**"Born of water and the Spirit"**
In John 3:5, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one "can enter into the kingdom of God" unless born of water and the Spirit, a key text for the necessity of baptism. Methodists teach that baptism brings a person into the covenant of grace.

**Noah's Flood and circumcision as types**
In 1 Peter 3, baptism is compared to the Flood, through which eight people were saved in Noah's Ark. Colossians 2 links baptism to circumcision, so it is often called its New Testament counterpart, and Ephesians 4 speaks of "one Lord, one faith, one baptism."
